strengths: Identifies an intuitive and well-motivated limitation in decoder-only MLLM architectures, where autoregressive causal masking prevents earlier modalities (such as image prefix tokens) from attending to subsequent prompt instructions.
The proposed Modality-Mutual Attention (MMA) is parameter-free, simple to implement by altering attention masks during SFT, and introduces minimal training overhead compared to dual-order training.

Comprehensive evaluation across 12 diverse benchmarks (spanning general, knowledge, and vision-centric tasks) with controlled apples-to-apples comparisons against standard causal baselines, dual-order variants, and concentric causal attention (CCA).
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited. Modifying attention masks to enable non-causal or bidirectional cross-attention across prompt tokens (such as prefix-LM style attention, bidirectional visual-textual prefix attention, or full prefix cross-attention) is a well-established concept in Transformer architectures and multimodal models. The paper does not adequately contextualize MMA against standard prefix-LM attention (where all prompt tokens attend bidirectionally) or justify why image tokens should attend to text tokens while maintaining causal masking among themselves (Eq. 5).

Missing critical ablation: The paper fails to compare MMA against a fully bidirectional prompt mask (where all multimodal prompt tokens attend to one another bidirectionally, as standard in prefix-decoder models like T5/Prefix-LM/Fuyu). Without this comparison, it is unclear whether the specific asymmetric mask in Eq. 5 provides any advantage over standard bidirectional prefix attention.

The method cannot be applied during the pretraining stage due to information leakage under next-token captioning objectives (as acknowledged in Section 6.2). This creates a discrepancy between pretraining and SFT attention dynamics, limiting the theoretical generality and scalability claimed in the introduction.

In the scaling comparison (Table 2), AKI-4B lags noticeably behind contemporary open-source models of similar size (e.g., Qwen2-VL-2B, BLIP-3-4B, Phi-3-Vision-4B) on key benchmarks such as MathVista (32.1 vs. 48.0/44.8) and CV-Bench (62.1/71.8 vs. 66.2/75.4), weakening the claim of state-of-the-art capability at the ~3-4B scale.

strengths: Clear problem identification: The paper clearly articulates an architectural asymmetry inherent in standard decoder-only MLLMs, where placing visual tokens before textual prompt tokens under standard causal attention prevents visual representations from conditioning on question context.

Comprehensive benchmark suite: The authors evaluate across 12 diverse vision-language benchmarks covering general perception, knowledge/reasoning, and vision-centric tasks (e.g., MME, MMBench, SEED-Bench, MMMU, MathVista, POPE, CV-Bench).

Detailed documentation and reproducibility efforts: The appendix includes explicit hyperparameter configurations, dataset composition details, prompt templates for training and evaluation, and granular category-by-category score breakdowns.

Transparent discussion of limitations: The authors explicitly analyze why MMA cannot be straightforwardly applied during the pre-training captioning stage due to information leakage across text tokens.
weaknesses: Omission of critical architectural baselines: The most standard way to allow cross-modal conditioning in decoder models during prompt processing is prefix attention (full bidirectional attention over the prompt tokens $[V, T_Q]$). The paper only compares against standard causal masking, Concentric Causal Attention (CCA), and an ad-hoc Dual-Order Training (DOT). Ablations comparing MMA against (1) standard bidirectional prompt attention and (2) bidirectional attention within visual tokens are missing.

Lack of principled justification for the attention mask structure in Equation 5: In Equation 5, image tokens are kept causal with respect to preceding image tokens ($j \le i$), and question tokens are causal with respect to preceding question tokens ($j \le i$), while image tokens can attend forward to question tokens. Because visual tokens represent a 2D spatial grid rather than a temporal sequence, and the question is entirely known ahead of generation, it is unclear why intra-modality causal masking is enforced rather than fully bidirectional intra-modality attention.

Unaddressed positional embedding dynamics (RoPE): The LLM backbone used throughout the paper is Phi-3.5-mini, which relies on Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE). In autoregressive causal LLMs, queries only attend to keys at positions $j \le i$ ($j - i \le 0$). Enabling image tokens ($1 \le i \le |V|$) to attend to question tokens ($j > |V|$) introduces positive relative position differences ($j - i > 0$) that the pretrained LLM weights have never encountered. The manuscript does not discuss how position indices or RoPE are handled.

Overstated comparative claims against state-of-the-art models: Section 4.3 and the abstract claim superior performance over comparable models. However, inspecting Table 2 reveals that AKI-4B underperforms BLIP-3-4B (which shares the identical underlying architecture: Phi-3.5-mini, SigLIP, and Perceiver Resampler) across most benchmarks, including MMB (73.1 vs. 76.0), SEED (69.4 vs. 71.8), MMMU (38.7 vs. 40.1), MathVista (32.1 vs. 40.1), RealWorldQA (58.9 vs. 61.6), and CV-Bench (62.1/71.8 vs. 66.2/75.4).

Anomalous degradation in the Dual-Order Training (DOT) baseline: In Table 1, introducing DOT causes severe performance drops on major benchmarks such as MMBench (dropping from 64.9 down to 43.8) and SEED (from 64.1 to 54.7). The manuscript attributes this vaguely to position confusion, but such drastic collapses suggest potential training instability or suboptimal prompt formatting that warrants deeper diagnosis.

strengths: Clear motivation: Addressing the limitation of strictly causal attention over prompt sequences (where earlier visual tokens cannot attend to later textual query tokens) is a relevant and practical topic in multimodal LLM research.
Comprehensive benchmark suite: The authors evaluate across 12 diverse benchmarks spanning general VQA, knowledge-intensive tasks, and vision-centric/spatial reasoning benchmarks.
Detailed appendix: The appendix provides useful implementation parameters, prompt templates, and category-level breakdowns across multiple benchmarks.
weaknesses: Overstated novelty and lack of crucial baselines: The concept of relaxing causal masking on the input prefix (prefix language modeling / non-causal prompt attention) is well established in transformer literature (e.g., UniLM, T5, UL2, PaLI). The proposed Modality-Mutual Attention (MMA) is effectively an asymmetric variant of prefix attention. Crucially, the authors do not compare MMA against standard bidirectional prefix attention (where all prompt tokens, both image and text, attend to each other bidirectionally), leaving it unclear whether MMA's specific asymmetric masking offers any advantage over standard prefix masking.

Claims contradicted by experimental results: The authors repeatedly claim in the Abstract, Introduction, and Section 4.3 that AKI-4B achieves 'superior performance compared to both open-source and proprietary models of similar size across most benchmarks.' However, Table 2 directly contradicts this claim: AKI-4B is outperformed by BLIP-3-4B across almost all evaluated benchmarks (MMBench: 73.1 vs. 76.0; SEED: 69.4 vs. 71.8; MMMU: 38.7 vs. 40.1; MathVista: 32.1 vs. 40.1; RealWorldQA: 58.9 vs. 61.6; CV-Bench 2D: 62.1 vs. 66.2; CV-Bench 3D: 71.8 vs. 75.4). It is also surpassed on multiple benchmarks by the smaller Qwen2-VL-2B.

Unexplained anomalies and potential issues in baselines: In Table 1, the Dual-Order Training (DOT) baseline suffers catastrophic degradation on multiple benchmarks (e.g., MMB drops by over 21 points to 43.8, SEED drops by ~10 points to 54.7), which strongly suggests issues in the training recipe rather than an inherent limitation of training with varied modality orders. Additionally, in Table 8, AKI-4B's Relation Reasoning (RR) score is listed as 0.65% (compared to ~67% for other configurations), which appears to be either a severe model failure or an unverified reporting error.

Omission of practical serving implications: In modern MLLM serving engines (e.g., vLLM, prompt caching architectures), caching precomputed visual KV activations across multiple queries or dialogue turns is a critical efficiency feature. By making image token representations conditioned on subsequent question tokens, the KV cache of visual inputs cannot be reused across questions. This practical trade-off is neither analyzed nor acknowledged.

Presentation and formatting defects: In the Abstract, the code repository URL is entirely missing ('available at , and we will release...'). In Table 1, the improvement row displays '-' for RealWorldQA rather than reporting the actual negative delta (-0.8%).
